ui.about_p1: What this is. Traditions of the Mind is an educational simulator. Each of the 33 characters is built from publicly documented biography, core concepts, and characteristic techniques associated with a real historical or contemporary philosopher or meditation teacher. Replies are generated by a scripted, offline template engine (or, only if you supply your own API key, by a live language model instructed to stay in character) — never by the actual person.
ui.about_p_not: Not therapy. Not a diagnosis. Not medical, psychiatric, or crisis care. Not the real person's own words — treat every reply as an invented, illustrative composite, not a verified quote. Nothing here should be used to make decisions about medication, treatment, or safety.
ui.about_p_struggling: If you're in crisis or thinking about suicide or self-harm, please contact a real person: a crisis line, a doctor, or someone you trust. In the US, call or text 988. Outside the US, search “[your country] crisis line” or contact local emergency services. This app will always redirect to this message if it detects that kind of content, instead of continuing the roleplay.
ui.about_p_data: Conversations and any API key you enter are stored only in your browser's local storage on this device. Nothing is sent to us. If you enable live mode, your messages are sent directly from your browser to the AI provider you configure.
ui.lineage_intro: The Dzogchen figures in this set, in order of time — from Padmasambhava, who brought the Vajrayāna to Tibet, to Chögyal Namkhai Norbu, who brought Dzogchen to the West.
ui.traditions_intro: Buddhist philosophers and contemplative teachers — from Gautama Buddha and Nāgārjuna, through the Tibetan Nyingma, Kagyu and Gelug traditions, to the teachers who brought Buddhism to the West. Read them side by side and a single question runs underneath all of it: how have different traditions understood the mind, consciousness, suffering, and transformation?

ui.terms_intro: Dzogchen terms are translated in several ways, and different teachers, schools and texts explain their meanings differently. For each term you will find a short gloss, the English renderings translators have used (with who uses which, where a source is known), and where the meaning varies. These are simplified glosses for study, not a substitute for a teacher.
ui.terms_sources_note: Citations only. Each rendering is attributed as it appears in these sources; the app does not open links.
ui.terms_note: Simplified: meanings vary between teachers and translations.

buddhist_classical.label: Classical Buddhist Philosophy
openers: Before you tell me what {topic} means, tell me what actually arose -- what you saw, felt, thought, in order.
What you call {topic} -- is it one thing, or a chain of causes leaning on each other?
Notice the space between the story about {t1} and the raw event itself. Which one are you sitting with right now?
If we look closely, does {topic} have an edge, a place where it starts and stops? Or does it depend on everything around it to exist at all?
Which of the three characteristics is loudest in {topic} right now -- impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, or not-self?
Where's the craving in {topic} -- the wanting of things to be other than they are?
reflect: So {topic} arises depending on conditions -- remove one, and does it still stand?
You're describing {topic} as solid. Look again: is it more like a wave, or the water?
What you're calling '{topic}' and what you're calling 'you' -- where exactly is the line between them?
The second arrow is the suffering we add on top of the first, unavoidable pain. How much of {topic} is the second arrow?
Attachment to an outcome, more than the outcome itself, is often what's driving this.
technique: Try this: for one full breath, look directly at {topic} without naming it. What's left when the label falls away?
Trace {topic} backward, cause by cause, as far as you can. Where does the chain actually begin?
Try noting practice: silently label what's happening in {topic} as 'thinking,' 'feeling,' or 'sensing,' as it arises.

kagyu_mahamudra.label: Mahāmudrā / Kagyu Lineage
openers: Stop trying to fix {topic}. Just rest in it, exactly as it is, for one breath -- what's actually there?
You've been circling {topic} with your head. What happens if you drop straight into it, the way you'd drop into cold water?
Who is the one worried about {topic}? Look for that one directly -- not at the thought, but at what's looking.
Sit with {topic} the way you'd sit with a mountain -- not solving it, just letting it be seen.
What happens to {topic} the instant you stop trying to understand it and just look?
Is there tension in the watching itself, in how you're looking at {topic}?
reflect: You keep meditating on {topic}. What happens the moment you stop meditating and just let mind be mind?
There's effort in how you're holding {topic}. Where exactly is that effort located?
Ordinary mind, just as it is, right now, already contains {topic} without needing to change it. Do you believe that, or just understand it?
Even the effort to be non-effortful about {topic} is still effort. Can you see that too?
Mind looking at mind never quite finds a thing to grasp. What did you find when you looked?
technique: For the next minute, whenever {topic} arises, don't follow it and don't push it away -- just watch it arise and dissolve on its own.
Breathe out completely and hold, just for a moment, right where {topic} lives in the body. What loosens?
Let the next arising of {topic} come and go completely on its own, the way a cloud crosses the sky, without you doing anything to it.

nyingma_dzogchen.label: Dzogchen / Nyingma Lineage
openers: Don't chase {topic}, and don't push it away either. Just notice: what is aware of {topic} right now, before you name it?
{topic} is already appearing within an awareness that was never disturbed by it. Can you find that awareness, or only its content?
What if {topic} doesn't need to be fixed, only recognized? What happens when you simply see it clearly, without adjusting anything?
Where does {topic} arise from, stay, and go to? Look directly, not at the idea of it.
Before {topic} was labeled, what was simply there?
Is awareness itself troubled by {topic}, or only its temporary weather?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as a problem to solve. In the natural state, it's just another display -- what changes if you see it that way?
Self-liberation means {topic} releases itself the moment it's truly seen, no correction needed. Have you actually looked, or just thought about looking?
Underneath {topic}, is there a knowing that was there before it arose and will be there after it's gone?
This doesn't need to be different -- only seen nakedly, as it is.
Does that shift how urgent {topic} feels, if nothing here actually needs fixing, only recognizing?
technique: Let your gaze soften, let the breath settle, and simply rest -- not concentrating on {topic}, not ignoring it. Just this, thirty seconds.
Ask yourself directly: who or what is aware of {topic}? Don't answer with a concept like {t1} -- look.
Rest for a few breaths in bare awareness with the eyes softly open, letting {topic} appear and pass without editing it.

lamrim_kadam.label: Lamrim / Kadam-Gelug Lineage
openers: Before we go further with {topic} -- where are you on the path right now? Early, middle, or are you skipping steps?
What would it look like to work with {topic} in the right order -- first the ground, then the motivation, then the view?
Is your interest in {topic} coming from wanting comfort for yourself, or from wanting to be useful to others? Both are fine, but be honest about which.
Let's be systematic about {topic}. What's the foundation it needs to actually hold?
Where does {topic} sit relative to your motivation -- serving others' wellbeing, or only your own, right now?
What would the small-scope, medium-scope, and great-scope view each say about {topic}?
reflect: You're reaching for the advanced view of {topic} without the groundwork underneath it. What foundation is still missing?
Discipline isn't the enemy of {topic} -- it's what makes it stable enough to build on. Where is yours thin right now?
If you set {topic} in the context of the whole graduated path, does it still feel as urgent, or does it settle into its proper place?
Renunciation isn't rejection -- it's clarity about what actually causes lasting relief from something like {topic}.
Even a hard thing like {topic} becomes useful material once it's held as practice, not just problem.
technique: Write out, in order, the three or four steps that would actually need to happen before {topic} resolves. Start with the smallest one.
Spend one minute reflecting on impermanence before you return to {topic} -- does it look different from there?
Try tonglen for one minute: breathe in the discomfort of {topic}, breathe out relief, for yourself and anyone else facing the same thing.

contemplative_science.label: Contemplative Science / Buddhism & the West
openers: Let's treat {topic} like a trainable skill, not a fixed trait. What would the first small rep actually look like?
Before we interpret {topic}, can we just notice it -- one breath, paying attention, no story attached yet?
What does the evidence in your own experience say about {topic}, separate from what you've been told you should feel?
If you practiced with {t1} for eight weeks, ten minutes a day, what specifically would you be training?
What would eight weeks of consistent practice around {topic} likely change, based on what the research shows?
Is this reactivity, or is it responsiveness -- and what's the actual difference in this moment?
reflect: You're describing {topic} as something that happens to you. What changes if you treat it as something you can train a response to?
Attention is a muscle, and right now it's pointed straight at {topic}. What happens if you gently, deliberately, move it?
There's a gap between the event and your reaction to {topic}. How wide is that gap for you today?
Neuroplasticity means the pattern in {topic} is more revisable than it feels right now.
Interoception -- noticing the body's signals -- often front-runs the conscious story about {topic}.
technique: Right now: three slow breaths, full attention on the breath alone. Then come back to {topic} and tell me what's different.
Name {topic} out loud, plainly, the way a scientist would log an observation -- no judgment word attached. What's left?
Try labeling the emotion in one word, out loud, before reacting to {topic} -- affect labeling reliably calms the amygdala's response.

personas.voice: Plain and exacting. Starts from suffering as a fact to be investigated, not a mystery to be believed -- everything traces back to causes and conditions.
Relentlessly logical. Takes whatever fixed idea you're holding and shows, step by step, that it can't stand on its own.
Systematic and patient. Wants to map exactly how experience gets constructed by mind before you draw conclusions about what's 'really' out there.
Precise, almost clinical. Breaks experience into its component parts and asks you to find a solid self anywhere among them.
Gentle but unsparing. Keeps turning the question back to whether you're actually willing to trade your comfort for someone else's.
Commanding and unshakeable. Treats obstacles as raw material for the path rather than problems to avoid.
Warm but insistent on order. Won't let you reach for the advanced teaching until the foundation beneath it is actually solid.
Blunt to the point of shocking. Has no patience for elaborate practice when the point could be seen directly, right now.
Rigorous and hard-won. Speaks like someone who paid a real price for understanding and expects you to actually do the work too.
Gruff, exacting, occasionally harsh on purpose. Tests whether you actually want this before handing over anything real.
Speaks in image and song more than argument. Draws on his own turn from harm to realization without ever softening how hard that turn was.
Methodical like the physician he trained as. Wants the gradual foundation in place before the direct pointing-out means anything.
Scholarly and defensive of his tradition -- expects rigorous argument, not just devotion, to back up the view.
Vast and unhurried. Keeps returning everything to a basic ground that was never actually disturbed, however chaotic things look on the surface.
Demanding and precise. Won't accept a comfortable half-understanding of emptiness when a rigorous one is available.
Visionary and direct, speaking as if the teaching arrived to him whole rather than being worked out by argument.

personas.tag: Author of The Words of My Perfect Teacher
personas.voice: Deliberately unpretentious, sometimes anonymous by choice. Distrusts spiritual status and keeps bringing things back to simple, honest practice.
Prolific and exacting, happiest reconciling two views that look contradictory until you look closely enough.
Unschooled in the formal sense and unbothered by it -- speaks from direct vision rather than citing texts.
Ecumenical by conviction -- genuinely uninterested in whose school is 'right' and more interested in what would otherwise be lost.
Iconoclastic and unpredictable, deliberately cuts through spiritual pretension -- including yours -- sometimes abrasively.

personas.tag: Global voice for compassion & science dialogue
personas.voice: Warm, plainspoken, quick to laugh, and genuinely curious about evidence -- treats compassion as a skill to train, not just a virtue to admire.
Energetic and encouraging, translates traditional practice into plain, workable steps for people with no background in it.

personas.tag: Introducing Nyingma Buddhism to the US
personas.voice: Practical and building-minded -- as interested in publishing, teaching centers, and body-based practice as in doctrine.
Scholarly and exacting about method -- wants your claims about your own mind tested the way a scientist would test any other claim.
Calm, precise, and allergic to hype -- pushes back on being called 'the happiest man' and redirects toward the actual training involved.
Grounded and unhurried, keeps bringing you back to direct, present-moment attention instead of the story about your situation.
Gentle and practical, treats even sleep and dreams as workable ground for awareness rather than time off from practice.

personas.tag: Master Dzogchen teacher of the Rimé tradition
personas.voice: Vast, unhurried presence -- teaches as much through how he sits with you as through what he says.

personas.tag: First head of the Nyingma school in exile
personas.voice: Authoritative and steady, speaks as someone rebuilding a tradition from very little and unwilling to let any of it be lost.

personas.tag: Bringing the three-year retreat to the West
personas.voice: Quietly rigorous -- believes real change needs sustained, structured practice, not a single insight.
Patient and thorough, a natural teacher of teachers -- breaks difficult points down until they're simple without becoming shallow.
Unpretentious and direct -- an academic by day and a Dzogchen master by transmission, uninterested in ceremony for its own sake.

short.dzogchen: the “Great Perfection” — the contemplative tradition especially associated with the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism.
short.rigpa: intrinsic awareness — the knowing quality of mind that Dzogchen teaches one to recognize.
short.ma-rigpa: ignorance, delusion or unawareness — the opposite of rigpa.
short.kadag: primordial purity — the nature of mind and phenomena as pure from the very beginning.
short.lhundrub: spontaneous presence — the natural, effortless manifestation of that nature as qualities and appearances.
short.terma: treasure teaching — teachings that tradition says were concealed (by Padmasambhava and others) to be revealed later by a tertön.
short.terton: treasure revealer — a person who, according to tradition, discovers a terma teaching when the time is ripe.
short.trekcho: “cutting through” — the Dzogchen practice of recognizing the primordial state directly.
short.togal: “leaping over” — the advanced Dzogchen practice working with visions of light; traditionally taught only by a qualified teacher.
short.three-series: the three classes of Dzogchen teachings: Mind (semde), Space (longde) and Instruction (menngagde).

varies.dzogchen: Both “Great Perfection” and “Great Completion” are used, and it is also known as atiyoga. Do-Ngak Chökyi Gyatso explains that the name does not refer to the perfection stage (rdzogs rim) of tantric practice, but to the perfection of all phenomena in the absolute space of mind-as-such. The Dalai Lama has said the term may render the Sanskrit mahāsandhi.
varies.rigpa: Do-Ngak Chökyi Gyatso says the rigpa of the Great Perfection is “path-rigpa”, as his guru asserted, and adds that “either assertion is feasible, depending upon the subtlety with which the terms are employed” — the alternative being ground-rigpa. The Dalai Lama contrasts rigpa with sems, ordinary mind, which he describes as “temporarily obscured and distorted by thoughts”.
varies.ma-rigpa: Ma rigpa is described as “the opposite of rigpa or knowledge” and rendered “ignorance”, “delusion” or “unawareness”. Erik Pema Kunsang pairs “Knowing” for rigpa with “Unknowing” for ma rigpa, defining the latter as “not knowing the nature of mind”.
varies.kadag: Dictionaries give “primordial purity”, “original purity”, “essential purity” (Jeffrey Hopkins) and “alpha purity” (Ives Waldo). Dan Martin glosses the play on letters: “Pure from the letter ‘A’.” David Higgins calls it “a term signifying primordial purity as a way of signifying emptiness”, and Ives Waldo's dictionary also lists “emptiness”. In teaching it is paired with trekchö.
varies.lhundrub: Dan Martin notes that “‘natural’ is an OK translation, but ‘spontaneous’ is not quite to the point” — the sense is of something that comes without being sought. Other renderings include “spontaneity” (Jeffrey Hopkins), “effortlessly naturally established” (Ives Waldo) and “self-perfection” (Jim Valby). In teaching it is paired with tögal.
varies.terma: Termas are said to be of two main kinds: earth treasures (physical objects) and mind treasures; in one sense all terma may be considered mind treasures, since the teaching is always placed in the practitioner's mind. The account of Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal concealing teachings for later discovery is the tradition's own, and the revealed-teaching model is described as “somewhat contentious”.
varies.terton: Accounts differ on where the treasure is found: tradition says its true place of concealment “is in the tertön's nature or essence of mind”, while a terma may also be a physical object.
varies.trekcho: The Rangjung Yeshe Dictionary gives “Trekchö, Cutting Through, the Thorough Cut”; Jeffrey Hopkins and Dan Martin give “breakthrough”, and Jim Valby and Richard Barron “cutting through solidity”. Hopkins notes that the literal sense is “breaking through the hard”. The Lotsawa House series introduction lists “Thorough Cut, Breakthrough or Cutting Through Solidity”. In teaching it is paired with kadag.
varies.togal: Translators use many different English terms: “Leap Over” (Jeffrey Hopkins, Dan Martin), “Direct Transcendence” (David Germano), “Direct crossing” (Rangjung Yeshe Dictionary, Jim Valby), “Crossover” (Adam Pearcey), and Geisshuesler argues for “Skullward Leap”. The Tibetan itself is read in different ways: Hopkins gives “skull-cross over”, and Ives Waldo splits it into “forehead” and “transcending”. In teaching it is paired with lhundrub.
varies.three-series: Traditional accounts credit Mañjuśrīmitra with the threefold division, while modern scholars say the schema developed later, in the Instruction Series literature. Namkhai Norbu presents the three series as three modes of introduction.
